what: Scott–Russell straight-line linkage. One motor moves a horizontal rack. A long bar is pinned to that slider at A, and a counterbalanced rocker pivots at fixed O. Its 32mm working arm OM reaches the long bar midpoint M and is exactly half the 64mm span AB. The rocker extends past O in the opposite direction to carry two real counterweight beams. In this planar mechanism the free tip B follows a perpendicular straight line, although it has no vertical guide. The same bar therefore carries three different paths: A on a horizontal line, M on a circular arc and B on a vertical line. The finite experiment visits seven positions and returns home. Exact straightness is an ideal geometric prediction; follow the free tip to compare its actual motion.
try: Open Examples and choose Line Turner, then open the model with its program. The model, Code and Blocks load together. Press Reset, then Run. Reset again before repeating or after manual movement; keep manual overrides off during the experiment.

Follow the three points of the long bar. A is attached to the horizontal rack, M is its midpoint at the end of the rocker working arm, and B is the free end. Find the counterweight on the other side of O. Then find the actual horizontal guides, then check that there is no vertical guide at B. The long bar changes orientation while its tip travels vertically; this is not a platform that stays level.

Stages 0–3 reduce the horizontal A coordinate from 57.6 to 51.2, 44.8 and 38.4mm, measured from O. Stages 4–6 return through 44.8, 51.2 and 57.6mm. Each move allows one second to settle and then a two-second teaching dwell. Watch the free tip rise and return while the midpoint swings around O.

The ideal tip heights above O are 27.897, 38.400, 45.705 and 51.200mm. The input moves 19.2mm over the lifting stroke and the tip rises 23.303mm. These are calculated values, not readings from the simulation. Compare actual body-carried points with the values rather than treating the motor target as an output measurement.

The variable sliderTargetMm is the horizontal coordinate of A from O. The motor uses the measured encoder sign only to position that rack: a 12-tooth pinion of 6mm pitch radius turns by 61.1155° for each 6.4mm step. A completed run ends with completed = 1, failed = 0, stage = 7 and arrived = 0, and the input motor holds home. Reset before another run after a manual move or an interrupted experiment.
why: Let O be the origin, A=(x,0), B=(u,h), and M=(A+B)/2. The bar length is AB=64mm and the rocker working arm is OM=32mm. Therefore |A+B|²=4|OM|²=64² and |B−A|²=|AB|²=64². Subtracting gives 4 A·B=0. Since x is nonzero, u=0. The actual planar pin joints keep B in the linkage plane, so its remaining motion is a vertical line. On the selected upper branch, x²+h²=64² and h=sqrt(64²−x²). M follows the circle |OM|=32mm. The rocker extension and counterweight leave these working lengths unchanged. The motor commands the horizontal input only; these paths are consequences of the passive links and joints.
matters: A mechanism can generate a straight output path without placing a straight guide on that output. Here the working lengths OM=AM=MB replace a second perpendicular slider with a rotating link. Straight Eight already shows an exact line through Peaucellier inversion, while Stride Lab gives an approximately straight coupler path; this experiment uses the exact isosceles sliding-block form often associated with Scott–Russell. Its useful question is how the constraint arrangement creates the line. The height law is also shared by a simple scissor lift, so unequal height increments alone are not the novelty. No force, efficiency, load capacity or real LEGO accuracy is established by this geometry.
question: A stays on a horizontal guide, but B has no vertical guide. Why can B still follow a vertical line, and what path does the midpoint M follow?
answer: Because the working distance OM is half AB and M is the midpoint, the two equal squared-length equations give A·B=0. For a nonzero horizontal A, B must have zero horizontal coordinate. The planar joints leave B on a vertical line, while M stays 32mm from O and follows a circular arc. The bar itself rotates; straight tip motion does not imply a fixed bar orientation.
further: Measure the actual horizontal slider coordinate and actual tip height independently. Test x²+h²=64² using those measurements, then check the tip distance from its declared vertical line. A point frozen on that line would pass straightness alone, so also require the full useful stroke and return.

Compare Ellipsa or Ellipse Engine: both have two perpendicular sliders. Which physical constraint in Line Turner replaces the second slider, and why does the midpoint trace a circle in both arrangements?

Predict the vertical increments for the three equal 6.4mm inward moves. Explain why the increments shrink even though all motor steps have equal magnitude. Keep this prediction separate from the exact-line argument.

Keep the declared route away from x=0 and x=64mm. At x=0 the perpendicular-line argument loses uniqueness; at x=64mm the upper and lower branches meet. The software envelope and the actual mechanical stops are different boundaries; inspect the stops and remain inside the demonstration route.

Explain why extending the rocker beyond O and adding a counterweight can reduce gravity-driven startup drift without changing the ideal A/M/B paths. The working pivot distances determine the geometry; the added mass changes the dynamics. Observe how it settles before starting the program.
formula: AB=64mm; working arm OM=32mm (the rocker also extends past O); M=(A+B)/2; A=(x,0), B=(u,h). |A+B|²=4|OM|²=|B−A|² ⇒ 4 A·B=0 ⇒ u=0 for x≠0. On the selected planar upper branch: h=√(64²−x²), M=(x/2,h/2). Input route x=[57.6,51.2,44.8,38.4,44.8,51.2,57.6]mm. Ideal heights=[27.896953,38.4,45.705142,51.2,45.705142,38.4,27.896953]mm. Inward rack travel s=6θ with θ in signed motor radians; actual motor sign is measured separately. Predicted coordinates never replace actual passive-point observations.
